For claim c1:
* **AP News** published an article on April 2, 2020, stating that the claim of hot water with lemon and bicarbonate of soda curing coronavirus is false. The article clarifies that this drink is not a cure for coronavirus and that there have been deaths attributed to the virus in Israel, contrary to some social media claims. It also quotes an infectious disease physician who states that no herbal remedies are recommended for COVID-19 and that nothing should be presumed to prevent or treat the virus unless it has gone through clinical trials. [1]
* **National Academies** published an article on April 22, 2020, explaining that consuming acidic drinks like lemon juice has no effect on coronavirus infections. It further states that lemon juice will not destroy viruses in the body or stop the virus-copying process, and that drinking the juice hot, with or without baking soda, will not prevent or cure a COVID-19 infection. [2]
* **The Guardian** reported on March 26, 2020, about "dangerous quack cures" for coronavirus being shared online, including lemon juice, liquid silver, and hot water. The article mentions that these remedies were being suggested in anti-vaccination Facebook groups and that the government advised reporting such content to social media companies. [3]
* **Times of Israel** published an article on April 5, 2020, debunking the false claim that Israel avoided coronavirus deaths by prescribing a mixture of hot water, lemon, and bicarbonate of soda. The article states that this claim is plainly false and that experts confirm there is no proof this or any herbal remedy will protect against COVID-19. [4]
* **CBS News** reported on May 5, 2020, that consuming acidic liquids like lemon juice will not kill the coronavirus. Dr. Mallika Marshall, in response to a viewer's question, emphasized that the best ways to protect oneself are social distancing, good handwashing, and taking good care of oneself. [5]
* **FactCheck.org** published an article on April 2, 2020, debunking a social media post that falsely claimed a blend of sodium bicarbonate and lemon juice would "eliminate" the novel coronavirus and had prevented COVID-19 deaths in Israel. The article states that this claim is baseless and that the World Health Organization confirmed there is no specific medicine recommended to prevent or treat the new coronavirus. [6]
